source_text: Si certum est denique nos nocentissimos esse, cur a vobis ipsis aliter tractamur, quam pares nostri, id est caeteri nocentes? cum ejusdem noxae eadem tractatio deberet intervenire. Quodcumque dicimur, cum alii dicuntur, et proprio ore et mercenaria advocatione utuntur ad innocentiae suae commendationem. Respondendi, altercandi facultas patet, quando nec liceat indefensos et inauditos omnino damnari. Sed Christianis solis nihil permittitur loqui, quod caussam purget, quod veritatem defendat, quod judicem non faciat injustum. Sed illud solum exspectatur quod odio publico necessarium est, confessio nominis, non examinatio criminis: quando si de aliquo nocente cognoscitis, non statim confesso eo nomen homicidae, vel sacrilegi, vel incesti, vel publici hostis (ut de nostris elogiis loquar) contenti sitis ad pronuntiandum, nisi et consequentia exigatis, qualitatem facti, numerum, locum, modum, tempus, conscios, socios. De nobis nihil tale, cum aeque extorqueri oporteret, quodcunque falso jactatur, quot quisque jam infanticidia degustasset, quot incesta contenebrasset, qui coci, qui canes affuissent. O quanta illius praesidis gloria, si eruisset aliquem, qui centum jam infantes comedisset! Atquin invenimus inquisitionem quoque in nos prohibitam. Plinius enim Secundus cum provinciam regeret, damnatis quibusdam Christianis, quibusdam gradu pulsis, ipsa tamen multitudine perturbatus, quid de caetero ageret, consuluit tunc Trajanum imperatorem, allegans praeter obstinationem non sacrificandi, nihil aliud se de sacramentis eorum comperisse, quam coetus antelucanos ad canendum Christo ut Deo et ad confoederandam disciplinam, homicidium, adulterium, fraudem, perfidiam, et caetera scelera prohibentes. Tunc Trajanus rescripsit, hoc genus inquirendos quidem non esse, oblatos vero puniri oportere. O sententiam necessitate confusam! Negat inquirendos ut innocentes, et mandat puniendos ut nocentes. Parcit et saevit, dissimulat et animadvertit. Quid temetipsum censura circumvenis? si damnas, cur non et inquiris? si non inquiris, cur non et absolvis? Latronibus vestigandis per universas provincias militaris statio sortitur; in reos majestatis et publicos hostes omnis homo miles est, ad socios, ad conscios usque inquisitio extenditur. Solum Christianum inquiri non licet, offerri licet, quasi aliud esset actura inquisitio, quam oblationem. Damnatis ergo oblatum; quem nemo voluit requisitum, qui, puto, jam non ideo meruit poenam, quia nocens est, sed quia, uon requirendus, inventus est. Itaque nec in illo ex forma malorum judicandorum agitis erga nos, quod caeteris negantibus adhibetis tormenta ad confitendum, solis Christianis ad negandum; cum, si malum esset, nos quidem negaremus, vos vero confiteri tormentis compelleretis. Neque enim ideo putaretis non requirenda quaestionibus scelera, quia certi essetis admitti ea ex nominis confessione, qui hodie de confesso homicida, scientes homicidium quid sit, nihilominus ordinem extorquetis admissi: quo perversius, cum praesumatis de sceleribus nostris ex nominis confessione cogitis tormentis de confessione decedere, ut negantes nomen pariter utique negemus et scelera, de quibus ex confessione nominis praesumpseratis. Sed, opinor, non vultis nos perire, quos pessimos creditis. Sic enim soletis dicere homicidae; Nega: laniari jubere sacrilegum, si confiteri perseveraverit. Si non ita agitis circa nocentes, ergo nos innocentissimos judicatis, cum quasi innocentissimos non vultis in ea confessione perseverare, quam necessitate, non justitia damnandam a vobis sciatis. Vociferatur homo: Christianus sum. Quod est dicit; tu vis audire quod non est. Veritatis extorquendae praesides, de nobis solis mendacium elaboratis audire. Hoc sum, inquit, quod quaeris, an sim; quid me torques in perversum? confiteor, et torques; quid faceres, si negarem? Plane aliis negantibus non facile fidem accommodatis; nobis, si negaverimus, statim creditis. Suspecta sit vobis ista perversitas, ne qua vis lateat in occulto, quae vos adversus formam, adversus naturam judicandi, contra ipsas quoque leges ministret. Nisi enim fallor, leges malos crui jubent, non abscondi; confessos damnari praescribunt, non absolvi. Hoc senatus consulta, hoc principum mandata definiunt, hoc imperium, cujus ministri estis. Civilis, non tyrannica dominatio ((vestra)) est. Apud tyrannos enim tormenta etiam pro poena adhibentur; apud vos soli quaestioni temperantur. Vestram illis servate legem usque ad confessionem; et si confessione praeveniantur, vacabunt. Sententia opus est; debito nocens expungendus est, non eximendus. Denique illum nemo gestit absolvere, non licet hoc velle; ideo nec cogitur quisquam negare. Christianum, hominem omnium scelerum reum deorum, imperatorum, legum, morum, naturae totius inimicum existimas, et cogis negare, ut absolvas, quem non poteris absolvere, nisi negaverit. Praevaricaris in leges. Vis ergo neget se nocentem, ut eum facias innocentem, et quidem invitum jam, nec de praeterito reum. Unde ista perversitas? ut etiam illud non recogitetis, sponte confesso magis credendum esse, quam per vim neganti; vel ne compulsus negare, non ex fide negarit; et absolutus ibidem post tribunal de vestra rideat aemulatione, iterum Christianus. Cum igitur in omnibus nos aliter disponatis, quam caeteros nocentes, id unum contendendo, ut de eo nomine excludamur (excludimur enim, si facimus, quae faciunt non Christiani), intelligere potestis non scelus aliquod in caussa esse, sed nomen, quod quaedam ratio aemulae operationis insequitur, hoc primum agens, ut homines nolint scire pro certo, quod se nescire pro certo sciunt. Ideo et credunt de nobis quae non probantur, et nolunt inquiri, ne probentur non esse, quae malunt credi esse, ut nomen illius aemulae rationis inimicum, praesumptis, non probatis criminibus, de sua sola confessione damnetur. Ideo torquemur confitentes, et punimur perseverantes, et absolvimur negantes, quia nominis praelium est. Denique quid de tabella recitatis illum Christianum, cur non et homicidam? Si homicida Christianus, cur non incestus? vel quodcunque aliud nos esse creditis? In nobis solis pudet aut piget ipsis nominibus scelerum pronuntiare? Christianus si nullius criminis reus est, nomen valde infestum, si solius nominis crimen est.
pass_a_gloss: If it is certain that we are the most guilty, why are we treated differently by you than our peers, that is, other guilty people, since the same treatment of the same fault ought to occur. Whatever we are said to be, when others are said to be, they use their own mouth and hired advocacy to commend their innocence. The ability to respond, to argue is open, when it is not permitted to condemn the undefended and unheard. But to Christians alone it is not permitted to speak what may purge the cause, what may defend the truth, what may not make the judge unjust. But only that is expected which is necessary for public hatred, confession of the name, not examination of the crime: when if you investigate someone guilty, you are not content with the confession of the name of homicide, or sacrilege, or incest, or public enemy (as I speak of our accusations), to pronounce, unless you also demand the consequences, the quality of the deed, the number, the place, the manner, the time, the accomplices, the associates. Of us nothing of this kind, when equally it ought to be extorted, whatever is falsely boasted, how many infanticides each has tasted, how many incests each has concealed, who were cooks, who were dogs. Oh how great is the glory of that governor, if he had uncovered someone who had already eaten a hundred infants! But we find that even investigation is prohibited against us. For Pliny Secundus, when he ruled the province, having condemned certain Christians, having repelled others from rank, nevertheless being disturbed by the very multitude, consulted then Emperor Trajan, alleging besides the obstinacy of not sacrificing, he had learned nothing else about their sacraments, except that they gathered before dawn to sing to Christ as God and to confirm discipline, prohibiting homicide, adultery, fraud, perfidy, and other crimes. Then Trajan wrote back, that this kind of people ought not to be investigated, but those who are brought forward ought to be punished. Oh, sentence confused by necessity! He denies that they ought to be investigated as innocent, and orders that they be punished as guilty. He spares and rages, dissimulates and takes notice. What are you doing to yourself with judgment? If you condemn, why do you not also investigate? If you do not investigate, why do you not also absolve? A military station is assigned to track down robbers throughout the provinces; every man is a soldier against enemies of majesty and public enemies, the investigation extends even to associates and accomplices. It is not permitted to investigate only the Christian, it is permitted to bring forward, as if the investigation would accomplish something other than the bringing forward. Therefore, having condemned, it is brought forward; which no one wanted to seek, who, I think, has not deserved punishment, because he is guilty, but because, not having been sought, he was found. And so you do not act towards us according to the form of judging evils, which you apply to others who deny, using torments to confess, to Christians alone to deny; since, if it were evil, we would deny, you would compel to confess with torments. For you do not think that crimes ought not to be investigated, because you are certain to admit them from the confession of the name, who today, having confessed to being a homicide, knowing what homicide is, nevertheless extort the order of admission: by which more perversely, when you presume crimes from the confession of the name, you compel with torments to depart from the confession, so that denying, we equally deny the name and the crimes, which you presumed from the confession of the name. But, I think, you do not want us to perish, whom you consider the worst. For thus you usually say to homicides: Deny, and I will order you to be torn apart, if you persevere in confessing. If you do not act thus towards the guilty, therefore you judge us to be most innocent, since you do not want us to persevere in that confession, which you know is to be condemned by necessity, not justice. A man cries out: I am a Christian. What he says, you want to hear what is not; you, the presidents of truth, labor to hear falsehood about us alone. This is what I am, he says, what you ask, whether I am; why do you twist me in the wrong direction? I confess, and you twist; what would you do, if I denied? Certainly to others who deny, you do not easily give faith; to us, if we deny, you immediately believe. Let that perversity be suspect to you, lest some force lie hidden, which serves you against the form, against the nature of judging, against the laws themselves. For unless I am mistaken, the laws order the evil to be punished, not hidden; they prescribe that the confessed be condemned, not absolved. This senatorial decree, these princely mandates define, this empire, whose ministers you are. Your domination is civil, not tyrannical. For among tyrants, torments are also used as punishment; among you, they are tempered only for questioning. Keep your law for them up to confession; and if they are anticipated by confession, they will be empty. A sentence is needed; the guilty ought to be expunged by debt, not exempted. Finally, no one strives to absolve him; it is not permitted to will this; therefore, no one is compelled to deny. You consider the Christian, a man accused of all crimes, enemy of gods, emperors, laws, morals, all nature, and you compel to deny, that you may absolve, whom you cannot absolve, unless he denies. You transgress the laws. You want him to deny that he is guilty, that you may make him innocent, and indeed unwilling, no longer guilty of the past. Whence is this perversity? So that you do not even consider that to one who confesses spontaneously, more faith ought to be given than to one who denies under force; or lest, compelled to deny, he does not deny from faith; and having been absolved, he may laugh at your rivalry, again a Christian, after the tribunal. When, therefore, you dispose of us differently in all things than other guilty people, contending for this one thing, that we be excluded from that name (for we are excluded, if we do what non-Christians do), you can understand that there is no crime in the cause, but the name, which a certain rival operation follows, first doing this, that men do not want to know for certain what they know for certain they do not know. Therefore, they also believe about us what is not proven, and they do not want to investigate, lest they be proven not to be what they prefer to believe they are, so that the name of that rival operation, with presumed, not proven crimes, may be condemned from its own confession alone. Therefore, we are tortured confessing, and punished persevering, and absolved denying, because it is a battle of the name. Finally, what do you recite from the tablet about that Christian, why not also about a homicide? If a Christian is a homicide, why not an incestuous person? Or whatever else you believe we are? In us alone is it shameful or irksome to pronounce the names of crimes? If the Christian is not guilty of any crime, the name is very hostile, if the crime is only of the name.

pass_b_english: Suppose we really are the worst criminals. Why, then, do you treat us differently from our peers — that is, from every other guilty person — when identical offenses demand identical handling? Other defendants speak for themselves or hire advocates to proclaim their innocence; the right to answer and to argue stands open because no one may be condemned without a defense or a hearing. Yet Christians alone are forbidden to say anything that could clear their case, uphold the truth, or keep the judge from acting unjustly. You demand only what public hatred requires: confession of the name, not examination of the crime. If you investigate a homicide or sacrilege or incest or treason, you are not satisfied with the mere admission of the label; you insist on the details — quality, number, place, manner, time, accomplices, associates. With us, nothing of the sort, even though it should be extracted with equal force: whatever is falsely alleged, how many infanticides each has tasted, how many incests each has concealed, which cooks and which dogs were present. Oh, the governor's glory if he could uncover someone who had already eaten a hundred infants! Yet we find that investigation itself is barred in our case.

When Pliny Secundus governed the province, he executed some Christians and stripped others of rank, but the sheer multitude unsettled him. He consulted Emperor Trajan, reporting that beyond their obstinate refusal to sacrifice he had discovered nothing about their rites except that they met before dawn to sing to Christ as God and to bind themselves by discipline against homicide, adultery, fraud, perfidy, and other crimes. Trajan replied that such people must not be sought out, but if brought before the court they must be punished. A verdict tangled by necessity! He denies they should be investigated as innocent, yet orders them punished as guilty. He spares and rages, feigns ignorance and takes notice. What are you doing to yourselves with this judgment? If you condemn, why not also investigate? If you will not investigate, why not also absolve? Military posts scour the provinces for robbers; every citizen becomes a soldier against enemies of the state, and inquiry reaches accomplices and associates alike. Only the Christian may not be investigated — only presented — as if investigation would produce anything but the presentation itself. So the accused is presented, then condemned — a man no one wanted to find, who, I suspect, earned punishment not because he was guilty but because, unsearched, he was discovered.

Thus you do not follow the standard form of judging crimes: you torture others who deny in order to extract a confession, but you torture Christians alone to force a denial. If Christianity were truly a crime, we would deny it and you would compel confession by torture. You do not think crimes should go uninvestigated because you are certain they are admitted by the mere confession of the name — yet even today, when a confessed murderer admits what murder is, you still extort a formal admission. More perversely still, you presume our crimes from the confession of the name, then use torture to make us withdraw that confession, so that in denying the name we equally deny the crimes you presumed from it.

I suspect you do not actually want us to perish, you who consider us the worst. You typically tell murderers: "Deny, and I will have you torn apart if you persist in confessing." If you do not act that way toward the guilty, then you judge us most innocent — since you do not want us to persist in a confession you know is condemned by necessity, not justice. A man cries, "I am a Christian." He tells you what he is; you want to hear what he is not. Presidents of truth, you labor to hear a lie from us alone. "This is what I am," he says, "the very thing you asked about. Why twist me the wrong way? I confess, and you twist. What would you do if I denied?" You hardly trust others who deny; us, if we deny, you believe at once. Let that perversity alarm you, lest some hidden force serve you against the form and nature of judgment, against the laws themselves. Unless I am mistaken, the laws order the guilty to be punished, not concealed; they prescribe that the confessed be condemned, not absolved. Senatorial decrees, imperial mandates, the empire whose ministers you are — all define this. Your rule is civil, not tyrannical. Under tyrants torture serves as punishment; under you it is reserved for questioning. Keep your law for them up to the point of confession; if confession forestalls it, the charge collapses. A sentence is required; the guilty must be removed by right, not excused. No one strives to absolve him; that is not permitted; therefore no one is compelled to deny.

You regard the Christian — a man charged with every crime, enemy of gods, emperors, laws, morals, all nature — and you compel him to deny so you can absolve a man you cannot absolve unless he denies. You transgress the laws. You want him to deny his guilt so you can make him innocent, and unwillingly so, no longer guilty of the past. Where does this perversity come from? So that you do not even reflect that a spontaneous confession deserves more credence than a forced denial; or that, compelled to deny, he does not deny from conviction; and once absolved, he may laugh at your rivalry, again a Christian, after leaving the tribunal. Since in everything you treat us differently from other criminals, insisting on this one point — that we be excluded from that name (for we are excluded if we do what non-Christians do) — you can see that the case involves no crime, but the name, which a certain rival doctrine pursues, first ensuring that men do not want to know for certain what they know for certain they do not know. Therefore they believe about us what is unproven, and refuse to investigate lest they prove we are not what they prefer to believe, so that the name of that rival doctrine, on presumed rather than proven crimes, may be condemned from its own confession alone. Hence we are tortured for confessing, punished for persisting, absolved for denying — because it is a battle over the name. Finally, why do you read "Christian" from the tablet, but not "homicide"? If the Christian is a homicide, why not "incestuous"? Or whatever else you believe we are? In us alone is it shameful or distasteful to pronounce the names of crimes? If the Christian is guilty of no crime, the name is intensely hostile — if the crime consists only of the name.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex legal and theological arguments of Tertullian. Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source. All nuances regarding the distinction between 'confessio nominis' (confession of the name) and 'examinatio criminis' (examination of the crime) are preserved. The translation of the Pliny/Trajan anecdote is faithful to the Latin syntax and meaning.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, with appropriate handling of the source material. The title 'Unfair Treatment of Christians' appropriately captures the central theme. The translation preserves the meaning, including the nuances of negation, agency, modality, and doctrine. Scripture citations are not present in the text, so no issues there.
